clinicalPearls: Symptomatic nervous-system involvement occurs in roughly 5-10% of sarcoidosis patients, though subclinical granulomas are more common at autopsy
Facial nerve palsy (often bilateral or recurrent) is the single most characteristic cranial neuropathy seen
Basilar leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI is a classic pattern, reflecting the predilection for meninges at the base of the brain
Hypothalamic-pituitary involvement can cause diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, or other endocrinopathies and should prompt pituitary axis testing
CSF findings are nonspecific — lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and sometimes low glucose — mimicking tuberculous or fungal meningitis
Neurologic disease can be the presenting manifestation of sarcoidosis before systemic disease is recognized, so tissue confirmation elsewhere (e.g., mediastinal nodes, skin) is valuable
Spinal cord involvement can mimic a longitudinally extensive myelitis or an intramedullary tumor on imaging
Response to immunosuppression supports but does not confirm the diagnosis, since some infections also transiently respond to steroids
harrison.pathophysiology: Neurosarcoidosis results from non-caseating granulomatous inflammation infiltrating the meninges, cranial nerves, hypothalamic-pituitary axis, brain parenchyma, or spinal cord. The granulomas provoke a perivascular and leptomeningeal inflammatory response that can cause direct compressive or infiltrative neurologic deficits, hydrocephalus from impaired CSF flow, or vasculopathy. Because it is part of a systemic multisystem granulomatous disease, isolated CNS presentations without other organ involvement are diagnostically challenging.
additionalDifferentials: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis or other granulomatous CNS disorders
additionalInvestigations: Brain and spine MRI with gadolinium — assesses leptomeningeal enhancement, parenchymal lesions, and cord involvement
CSF analysis with cell count, protein, glucose, ACE, and cytology — evaluates for lymphocytic pleocytosis and excludes malignancy/infection
Serum and CSF ACE levels — supportive but neither sensitive nor specific
Chest CT and/or whole-body FDG-PET — identifies occult systemic (especially thoracic) granulomatous disease for biopsy targeting
Tissue biopsy of an accessible extraneural site (lymph node, skin, lacrimal gland) — establishes histologic diagnosis of non-caseating granulomas
Pituitary hormone panel — screens for hypothalamic-pituitary axis dysfunction when relevant symptoms present
Ophthalmologic slit-lamp exam — detects concurrent uveitis supporting systemic sarcoidosis
Infectious workup (AFB stain/culture, fungal antigen, treponemal serology) on CSF — excludes key infectious mimics before immunosuppression
redFlags: Rapidly progressive myelopathy or brainstem signs suggesting need for urgent imaging and treatment
Hydrocephalus or signs of raised intracranial pressure from basilar meningeal involvement
Unexplained diabetes insipidus or panhypopituitarism in a patient with known or suspected sarcoidosis
New seizures or mass-like parenchymal lesions requiring exclusion of malignancy or infection before immunosuppressive therapy
Optic neuropathy, which can threaten vision and warrants prompt treatment
pitfalls: Starting empiric immunosuppression before adequately excluding infectious mimics (especially TB and fungal disease) can worsen unrecognized infection
Relying solely on elevated CSF or serum ACE for diagnosis, as this is neither sensitive nor specific
Assuming a favorable steroid response confirms sarcoidosis, since infections and other inflammatory conditions may also improve transiently
Overlooking neurosarcoidosis in a patient without known systemic sarcoidosis, since isolated CNS presentation occurs in a meaningful subset of cases
harrison.prognosis: Course is variable — many patients respond to immunosuppressive therapy with partial or complete resolution, but a subset experience chronic, relapsing, or progressive disease, particularly with parenchymal brain or spinal cord involvement, which carries a worse functional outcome.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Sarcoidosis chapter (Nervous System Involvement)
management: Induce remission with systemic corticosteroids, the first-line therapy for active neurosarcoidosis
Add a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate for prolonged control and to limit corticosteroid toxicity
Escalate refractory or severe parenchymal or spinal-cord disease to a TNF-alpha inhibitor such as infliximab

Replace deficient hormones for hypothalamic-pituitary involvement, using desmopressin for cranial diabetes insipidus and other pituitary hormone replacement, and control symptomatic seizures with antiepileptic drugs
Divert cerebrospinal fluid with a shunt for symptomatic hydrocephalus
Monitor disease activity and treatment response with serial neuroimaging and screen for corticosteroid and immunosuppressant complications
Manage within a multidisciplinary team spanning neurology, respiratory or sarcoidosis specialists, endocrinology and neurosurgery
